extracted.intended_audience: readers and students interested in the philosophy of education and 19th‑century essays (general educated readership)
extracted.subtask_description: Extract normative criteria and definitions of education and intellectual cultivation from 19th‑century essays (Huxley, Newman, and accompanying reflections). Focuses on what counts as education, the purpose of artificial education, characteristics of a liberal education, and the role of feeling and art in culture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of education
rubrics_metrics.description: Education is the instruction of the intellect in the laws of Nature, and the fashioning of the affections and of the will into an earnest and loving desire to move in harmony with those laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verbatim framing from Huxley: treat education as both cognitive instruction (laws of Nature, including 'men and their ways') and moral/affective formation (fashioning affections and will). Use this as the standard by which anything calling itself 'education' should be judged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for calling anything 'education'
rubrics_metrics.description: Anything which professes to call itself education must be tried by this standard [instruction in the laws of Nature and the fashioning of affections/will], and if it fails to stand the test I will not call it education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Huxley's explicit evaluative rule: programmes, schools, or practices should be assessed by whether they teach the laws governing phenomena and human nature and whether they cultivate affections and will oriented to those laws. Mere authority or numbers do not suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of artificial education
rubrics_metrics.description: Artificial education's object is to make good the defects in Nature's methods; to prepare the child to receive Nature's education, neither incapably nor ignorantly, nor with wilful disobedience; in short, all artificial education ought to be an anticipation of natural education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artificial (formal) schooling should anticipate and smooth natural experiential learning: teach preparatory knowledge/skills, inculcate habits so the learner recognizes Nature's rewards/penalties without suffering them first. Emphasize readiness for real‑world consequences rather than rote or ornamental instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of a liberal education
rubrics_metrics.description: A liberal education trains the body to be the ready servant of the will; makes the intellect a clear, cold, logic engine ready for any work; stores the mind with knowledge of the great and fundamental truths of Nature; trains the passions to come to heel by a vigorous will and a tender conscience; teaches love of beauty, hatred of vileness, and respect for others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Huxley lists these as the composite outcomes of a liberal education. Use them as multi‑dimensional criteria (physical self‑management, intellectual versatility, foundational knowledge, moral/self‑control, aesthetic sensibility, social respect). A programme claiming to deliver a 'liberal education' should show evidence against each element.

rubrics_metrics.name: No such thing as an uneducated person (nature as educator)
rubrics_metrics.description: In strictness, there is no such thing as an uneducated man: Nature educates continuously through experience (pain/pleasure, social relations), so education in some form begins immediately and never wholly ceases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating education, acknowledge the baseline of natural, experiential learning. Formal education should be assessed relative to this continuous background instruction and its capacity to correct or enhance nature's rough lessons rather than ignore them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Happiness and the proper aim of life (anti‑self‑consciousness principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Happiness is the test of all rules of conduct, but the end is best attained by not making it the direct end: only those are happy who have their minds fixed on some object other than their own happiness; aiming at something else (happiness of others, improvement of mankind, art/pursuit) they find happiness by the way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the autobiographical reflection: practical ethical guidance for education and character formation—teach aims and pursuits external to self‑conscious pursuit of happiness (public goods, art, vocation) so that happiness emerges incidentally. Use as a criterion when judging aims emphasised by curricula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivation of feeling alongside intellectual analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Passive susceptibilities (the feelings) need to be cultivated as well as active capacities (intellect and action); maintenance of a due balance among the faculties is of primary importance; the cultivation of the feelings became one of the cardinal points in the ethical and philosophical creed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate educational practice for balance: does it nourish emotions, sensibilities, and aesthetic appreciation as well as analytical skill? Programmes that emphasize analysis exclusively fail this criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of poetry, art, and music as instruments of culture
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry and art are instruments of human culture able to cultivate the feelings; music excites enthusiasm and sustains elevated feelings; Wordsworth's poems 'expressed, not mere outward beauty, but states of feeling, and of thought coloured by feeling' and thus function as medicine for a depressed mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider inclusion and weight of imaginative arts in an education: their capacity to create perennial sources of happiness and to cultivate sympathy/imaginative feeling is a specific evaluative dimension. Assess whether curricular use of arts aims to develop feeling and moral imagination, not mere technical appreciation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivation of the intellect as an end (Newman)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a need for a term expressing intellectual proficiency or perfection; cultivation of the intellect as an end is a legitimate object—distinct from raw talent (talent, ability, genius) and from practice‑oriented virtues (judgment, taste, skill); wisdom relates conduct to life, but the intellect itself can be cultivated as a state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newman's point is conceptual and evaluative: when designing or assessing education, distinguish between (a) raw gifts, (b) practical arts and skills, and (c) cultivation of the intellect as an intrinsic end (knowledge, science as intellect's subject matter). Use this distinction to judge whether programmes seek mere utility or intellectual perfection.
